prompt: Why does the budget hold bytes and request counts as well as timings?
hint: When does each kind of number move?

choices.text: Lighthouse cannot measure the timings unless a byte budget sits beside them
choices.why: Lesson 10 read every timing with no budget at all.

choices.text: They move in the diff that adds them, and stay steady between runs
choices.why: Right. A new library shows up in the script bytes before anybody times a phone.

choices.text: The Core Web Vitals themselves are defined in bytes downloaded on a phone
choices.why: They are defined in seconds, milliseconds and a unitless shift score.

choices.text: Bytes are what the field data in CrUX reports
choices.why: CrUX reports the three vitals from real visits, not page weight.

prompt: What is wrong with a budget that says only "performance score at least 0.9"?
hint: What the score is made of.

choices.text: A blend of five holds still while one metric crosses its threshold
choices.why: Right, and when it drops it does not say which change or which metric.

choices.text: Lighthouse 13 reports no score in its JSON
choices.why: It does, under categories.performance.score.

choices.text: 0.9 is too strict for a page with pictures
choices.why: The fixed page scored 1 with a picture on it.

choices.text: Scores are measured in the field, while budgets are checked in the lab
choices.why: The score is a lab number; it comes from the same Lighthouse run.

prompt: What does Lighthouse 13.5.0 itself offer for checking a budget?

choices.text: A --budget-path flag that reads a budget file
choices.why: Older versions had one; 13.5.0's help does not mention a budget.

choices.text: A performance-budget audit in the report
choices.why: The list of audits mentions no budget either.

choices.text: No budget flag and no budget audit, so the check is a script over the report
choices.why: Right. budget.py is that script.

choices.text: A budget category beside performance and accessibility
choices.why: The categories are accessibility, best-practices, performance, seo and agentic-browsing.

prompt: budget.py ends with an exit code of ___ when any line of the budget is over.
hint: The exit code a pipeline reads as a failure.

prompt: What does k6 do when a threshold fails?

choices.text: Stops at the first failed request and exits with code 1
choices.why: A threshold is judged at the end of the run, over the whole run.

choices.text: Finishes the run and exits with code 99
choices.why: Right, after reporting which threshold crossed. The exit code is what the gate counts.

choices.text: Prints a warning about it and exits with code 0
choices.why: Then no pipeline could fail on it.

choices.text: Runs the whole test again to confirm the failure
choices.why: Repeating is the gate's job; k6 runs once.

prompt: Why does api.js check the baseline as well as the 200 ms requirement?
hint: What happened when the index was dropped.

choices.text: The requirement is checked by Lighthouse, so k6 needs a number of its own
choices.why: Lighthouse measures pages; both thresholds in api.js are k6's.

choices.text: A baseline is cheaper to compute than a percentile
choices.why: The baseline is a percentile, recorded from earlier runs.

choices.text: It catches an endpoint that got much slower and stayed under 200 ms
choices.why: Right. The requirement passed and the baseline did not.

choices.text: k6 refuses a script with a single threshold
choices.why: One threshold is a perfectly valid script.

prompt: If baseline.json held a 95th percentile of 2 ms, what limit in milliseconds would api.js put in its second threshold?
Match each piece of the back end's gate to what it does.
hint: The notes beside api.js, and the baseline commands.

pairs.right: compares with the last accepted version
sends the same number of requests on every run
writes the run's metrics to a JSON file

prompt: Why was the baseline recorded as the median of three runs?
hint: What a baseline is compared against afterwards.

choices.text: k6 needs three summaries to exist before it can read even one of them
choices.why: Each run writes its own summary; one is readable on its own.

choices.text: A single run carries its own noise into every later comparison
choices.why: Right. A lucky or unlucky baseline makes every later verdict lucky or unlucky.

choices.text: The median of a set of runs comes out lower than the mean of the same runs
choices.why: It is less moved by one wild run, which is the point; it is not lower every time.

choices.text: Three runs warm the database cache
choices.why: The baseline is about noise between runs, not about warming anything.

prompt: gate.sh counts how many k6 runs failed instead of sorting the three 95th percentiles. Why is that the same verdict?
hint: A fixed limit, and three runs.

choices.text: With a fixed limit, the median crosses it exactly when at least two of the three runs do
choices.why: Right. With five runs the rule would be three.

choices.text: k6 sorts the runs itself before it exits
choices.why: Each k6 run knows nothing about the others.

choices.text: It is a different verdict, accepted because it is faster
choices.why: It is the same verdict, by arithmetic, and it costs no more.

choices.text: The exit code of 99 already holds the median of the runs
choices.why: The exit code of one run says only whether that run crossed a threshold.

prompt: Why does the tolerance in api.js carry an absolute part, 5 ms, beside the 50%?

choices.text: k6 thresholds reject a limit under 5 ms
choices.why: A threshold takes any number.

choices.text: On a 2 ms endpoint the noise is milliseconds, more than 50% of it
choices.why: Right. A relative tolerance alone would fail good changes on a busy machine.

choices.text: The absolute part is the 40 ms that the payment stand-in adds to a request
choices.why: GET /shows/{id} does not pay; only a booking does.

choices.text: It keeps the computed limit safely above the 200 ms requirement of lesson 1
choices.why: Baseline 1.5 times plus 5 ms stays far below 200 ms here.

prompt: Which of these habits keep a performance gate worth trusting? Pick every one that applies.
hint: The last part of the section.

choices.text: Run it on the same kind of machine every time
choices.why: Right. Otherwise a comparison measures the machines.

choices.text: Refresh the baseline when a change that should move it is accepted
choices.why: Right. Deliberately, and by somebody who knows why.

choices.text: Judge medians of several runs
choices.why: Right. One run is one sample.

choices.text: Rewrite the baseline from the result of every run
choices.why: A baseline that follows every run follows every regression too.

choices.text: Set the tolerance below the spread measured between runs
choices.why: Then the gate fails good changes, and people learn to rerun it.

prompt: Why does the workflow upload perf/runs/ with if: always()?
hint: When would the reports be needed most?

choices.text: GitHub deletes the runner's files unless they are uploaded twice
choices.why: Once is enough; always() is about when, not how often.

choices.text: The upload makes the gate pass on the next attempt
choices.why: Uploading changes no verdict.

choices.text: So that a failed gate still leaves the evidence of why
choices.why: Right. Without it a red job sends somebody to reproduce it by hand.

choices.text: Lighthouse refuses to write reports outside a workflow
choices.why: It wrote them on the VM, with no workflow at all.

prompt: The baseline in the repository was recorded on your VM, and the gate runs on a GitHub runner. What is wrong with that?
hint: What a comparison between two machines measures.

choices.text: The comparison measures the difference between the machines as much as the change
choices.why: Right. Record the baseline on the runner the gate uses.

choices.text: GitHub runners cannot run k6
choices.why: The workflow installs k6 the way lesson 5 does.

choices.text: JSON files written on a VM are unreadable on a runner
choices.why: JSON is the same text on both.

choices.text: The runner is faster, so the gate passes too easily
choices.why: It may be faster or slower; the trouble is that nobody knows which.

prompt: A team's performance gate fails good changes now and then, and passes when rerun. What is the cost?
hint: What people do with a red job they have learnt to distrust.

choices.text: Each rerun costs a few more minutes of runner time on the pull request
choices.why: That is the small cost. The large one is what the team learns.

choices.text: People rerun a red gate until it is green, and stop reading it
choices.why: Right. Then the real regression is rerun until it passes too.

choices.text: The baseline drifts upwards with each rerun
choices.why: The baseline moves only when somebody records a new one.

choices.text: Lighthouse stops trusting its own simulation after a run of failures
choices.why: Lighthouse keeps no memory between runs.

prompt: Put the steps of gate.sh in the order it runs them.
items: remove the reports of the last run
run Lighthouse three times on the page
check the medians of the three reports against the budget
run k6 three times on GET /shows/{id}
count the k6 runs that crossed a threshold
print the verdict and exit with it

prompt: The gate's budget lines are all ok, and its three k6 runs exit with 99, 0 and 99. What does the gate decide?
hint: Two of three, and what that says about the median run.

choices.text: Pass, because the front end was within budget
choices.why: The gate fails if either half fails.

choices.text: Fail: two of the three runs crossed, so the median run did
choices.why: Right. One quiet run does not outvote two that crossed.

choices.text: Pass, because one k6 run met every threshold
choices.why: One good run is one sample; the median is what the gate judges.

choices.text: It cannot decide until a fourth run is made to break the tie
choices.why: Three runs cannot tie, which is one reason to use an odd number.
